lesson.label: Technique: how to give and receive feedback

items: Could you have a quick look at...?
***Could you have a quick look at*** *my slides?*
I'd really appreciate a second opinion.
Is there anything I could do better?
First of all, ...
***First of all,*** *you've done a great job on the campaign.*
The part about... is spot on.
***The part about*** *delivery times* ***is spot on****.*
The only thing is, ...
***The only thing is****, the ending feels a bit sudden.*
There's one thing I wanted to mention, though.
a bit + adj
*Some slides are* ***a bit*** *text-heavy.*
It's not a huge problem, but...
***It's not a huge problem, but*** *it does hold up the team.*
Maybe you could + V
***Maybe you could*** *cut it down to three bullet points.*
It might be worth + V-ing
***It might be worth*** *adding a summary slide.*
That way, + clause
***That way****, they'll listen to you instead of reading.*
But overall, ...
***But overall****, it's really strong.*
Just so you know, ...
***Just so you know****, I'm really happy with your work.*
That's really helpful. / I appreciate the feedback.
Fair point. / I hadn't thought of that.
I'll make sure (that)... / From now on, I'll...
***I'll make sure*** *I flag it early* ***from now on****.*

lesson.label: 🧠 Brainstorming questions (Câu hỏi nên nghĩ trước buổi học)
items: When was the last time someone gave you **feedback at work or school? How did you feel?**
Do you **find it easier to give feedback or to receive it**? Why?
Is it common to **give direct feedback** in Vietnamese workplaces?
What makes **feedback helpful,** and what **makes it hurtful?**

lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Can I get a second opinion?
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Mia has a presentation with a new client tomorrow. She asks her colleague, Tom, to look at her slides.*
lines: Tom, have you got five minutes? Could you **have a quick look at** my slides for tomorrow? I'd really appreciate **a second opinion.**
And please **be honest**. **I'd rather hear it from you than** from the client.
Fair enough. OK, **first of all**, the design looks great. It's clean and professional, and the charts are really **easy to follow**.
**It shows.** **The only thing is**, some of the slides feel a bit **cluttered**. Like this one, there's a whole paragraph. I think you might **lose their attention**.
Yeah, **I had a feeling** that one was too much. **What would you do?**
**Maybe you could** **cut it down to** three bullet points and explain the rest **out loud**. **That way**, they'll **focus on** you instead of reading.
Hmm, the ending feels a bit **rushed**. You go straight from the prices to "Thank you." **It might be worth** adding a slide with **the key takeaways**, so you **end on a strong note**.
But honestly, **overall**, it's really **solid**. The part about delivery times is **spot on**. That's exactly what they care about. You've really **nailed** that bit.
**That's really helpful**, thanks. I'll **make a few tweaks** tonight and **run through it** one more time.
Sounds good. You'll be fine. Good luck tomorrow!

lesson.title: 2. The monthly one-to-one
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Sam has worked in the marketing team for six months. His manager, Laura, is having their monthly one-to-one meeting with him.*
lines: So, **how are things going** at the moment?
Pretty good, thanks. It's been **a busy month**, but I'm enjoying it.
**Good to hear.** **I wanted to start by saying** you've **done a great job on** the social media campaign. Our engagement has **gone up by** about 30% since you **took over**. That's **a big deal**.
Thanks, that's really nice to hear.

**There's one thing I wanted to bring up, though.** Your last two weekly reports came in a couple of days late. **It's not the end of the world**, but it does **hold up** the rest of the team, because they need your numbers for their own reports.
Ah, right. Sorry about that. To be honest, I've been **struggling to keep on top of** everything since the campaign started.
I get it. You've **got a lot on your plate** right now. Is there anything that would help?
Maybe if I knew the priorities a bit earlier in the week? Sometimes urgent tasks **come up** on Thursday, and then everything else **gets pushed back**.
**Okay.** I'll send you a list of priorities every Monday morning. And if you can see that a deadline is going to be **tight**, just **give me a heads-up**. We can always **work something out**.
That would really help. I'll make sure I **let you know** early **from now on**.
Great. And **just so you know**, I'm really happy with your work **overall**. This is just a small thing.
Thanks. I appreciate you **being upfront** about it.
Of course. Let's **check in** again next month and see how it's going.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Leo is giving a speech at his brother's wedding next weekend. He's practising it in front of his friend, Hana.
lines: So, what did you think? Please {be honest}. I'd rather hear it from you than from two hundred guests.
OK. I loved the story about the two of you getting lost in Đà Lạt. Honestly, you {nailed} that part. Everyone will laugh.
Really? I {spent ages on} that bit.
{It shows}. The only thing is, the speech is a bit long. It took nearly ten minutes.
Yeah, {I had a feeling} it was too long. {What would you do}?
Maybe you could {cut it down} to about five minutes. People get hungry at weddings!
The ending felt a bit {rushed}. You just said “Cheers!” and sat down. It might be worth saying something personal to the couple, so you {end on a strong note}.
Good idea. Anything else I should change?
No, overall it's really {solid}. Make a few tweaks, run through it a couple more times, and you'll be fine.

homework.title: Part 3: Choose the best response
homework.instructions: Choose the most natural and polite option.

questions.q: Your colleague asks for feedback on her report. It's good, but too long. What do you say first?
options: To be honest, the report is too long.
First of all, the research is really good. You must have spent ages on it.
The report is OK, but it's long.
questions.why: Start with something specific and positive before mentioning a problem.

questions.q: You want to mention a problem gently.
options: There's one thing I wanted to bring up, though.
I need to tell you about a big problem.
You always send your reports late.
questions.why: “There's one thing I wanted to bring up, though” introduces the problem softly.

questions.q: You want to suggest a solution.
options: You should cut it down.
Maybe you could cut it down to one page. That way, it's easier to read.
Cut it down, please.
questions.why: “Maybe you could…” is gentle, and “That way, …” explains the benefit.

questions.q: Someone gives you a useful idea you didn't think of.
options: OK, if you say so.
Good point. I hadn't thought of that.
Yes, I already knew that.
questions.why: It thanks the person and shows you value the idea.

questions.q: Your manager says your reports have been late.
options: Sorry, but I've been too busy.
Ah, right. Sorry about that. I'll make sure I let you know earlier from now on.
Other people are late too.
questions.why: Apologise and promise a clear change, without making excuses.

questions.q: You want to finish your feedback on a positive note.
options: But overall, it's really solid.
So that's everything that's wrong.
Anyway, just change those things.
questions.why: “But overall, it's really solid” ends the feedback positively.

homework.title: Part 4: Listening
homework.intro: Mai is a freelance designer. She's showing the first version of a new menu to Peter, who owns a small café. Listen, then answer the questions.

script.text: Thanks for sending this over. I had a good look at it last night.
Great. So, what do you think? Please be honest. It's only the first draft.
Well, first of all, I love the colours. The green and cream look really fresh, and ==they match the café perfectly==.
Oh, good. I spent ages choosing those.
It shows. The only thing is, the text is a bit small. ==A lot of our customers are older, and I think some of them would struggle to read it.==
That's a fair point. ==I was trying to fit everything on one page.==
I know. Maybe you could use two pages instead, one for drinks and one for food? That way, you can make the text bigger.
That makes sense. ==It'll cost a little more to print==, though. Is that OK?
That's fine. It's not a big difference.
Just one more thing. The photos of the cakes are lovely, but ==they're not actually our cakes==. Customers might be disappointed if the real ones look different.
Ah, I hadn't thought of that. Could you send me some photos of your cakes? ==Or I could come in and take some myself.==
==Could you come in on Saturday morning?== That's when everything's fresh.
Sure, Saturday works. ==I'll bring my camera.==
Perfect. Honestly, overall, I'm really happy with it. It looks much more professional than our old menu.
Thanks, that's good to hear. I'll make those changes and send you a new version by Wednesday.
Great. No rush. Just give me a heads-up if it's going to take longer.

questions.q: What does Peter think of the colours?
options: They're too bright for the café.
They suit the café very well.
He'd like a bit more green.

questions.q: Why does Peter want bigger text?
options: Some customers might find it hard to read.
The menu doesn't have enough items.
He wants to add more dishes.
questions.why: “Some of them would struggle to read it.”

options: Mai wanted to keep the printing cost low.
Mai tried to put everything on one page.
Peter had asked for a one-page menu.
questions.why: “I was trying to fit everything on one page.”

questions.q: What is the downside of Peter's suggestion?
options: It will take longer to design.
Printing will cost a bit more.
Customers won't like a two-page menu.
questions.why: “It'll cost a little more to print.”

questions.q: What's the problem with the cake photos?
options: They're the wrong size.
They don't show the café's real cakes.
They aren't very good quality.
Mai will send the new version of the menu.
Mai will take photos at the café.
Peter will send Mai some photos.
questions.why: “Could you come in on Saturday morning?” … “I'll bring my camera.”

homework.title: Part 5: Speaking (2 minutes)
homework.instructions: Choose ONE option and record yourself speaking for about 2 minutes. You are the only speaker.

options.title: (Story) Tell me about a time you had to give someone feedback.
questions: Who was it, and what was the feedback about?
How did you feel before you said it?
Would you say it differently now?
options.use: I wanted to start by saying…, There's one thing I wanted to bring up, though, It's not the end of the world, but…, Maybe you could…, overall.

options.title: (Give feedback) Choose ONE situation and give feedback, as if you're talking to the person.
choices: Your friend has opened a small restaurant. The food is delicious, but the service is very slow.
Your colleague has made a new company website. It looks modern, but it's hard to find the contact details.
A new team member wrote a very detailed report, but sent it two days late.
options.use: First of all, …, It shows, The only thing is…, It might be worth + V-ing, That way, …, spot on, solid.

options.title: (Opinion) Is it better to get feedback often, or only once or twice a year?
questions: How often do people get feedback where you work or study?
What are the good sides of regular feedback?
What would you prefer, and why?
options.use: check in with sb, give sb a heads-up, keep on top of sth, be upfront, I'd rather… than…, It depends on…
